episode.title: The Inca civil war and Spanish invasion
episode.who: Pedro Cieza de León and Inca Garcilaso de la Vega
episode.document: Pedro Cieza de León, The Discovery and Conquest of Peru; Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries of the Incas
episode.why: The two accounts clarify how succession conflict, imperial alliance, captive-taking, and Spanish intervention interacted instead of reducing Andean violence to ritual warfare.

dossier.text: 'As I noted the many great and strange things that are to be seen in the new world of the Indies there came upon me a strong desire to write an account of some of them, as well those which I have seen with my own eyes as those I heard of from persons of good repute.' In another place he says: 'Oftentimes when the other soldiers were sleeping, I was tiring myself in writing. Neither fatigue nor the ruggedness of the country, nor the mountains and rivers, nor intolerable hunger and suffering, have ever been sufficient to obstruct my two duties, namely, writing and following my flag and my captain without fault.'

There must, however, have been interpreters of the quipus, those who, with knowledge derived from other sources, could use the knots as reminders and suggesters by which an event could be kept in memory with more accuracy. These were the Amautas, or learned men and councillors. For them the quipus formed a system of reminders, giving accuracy to knowledge derived from other methods of recording events and traditions. For it cannot be supposed that the system of different coloured knots could do more than supply a sort of aid to memory, or a memoria technica. It is, however, certain that the traditions and records of events were preserved by the Amautas with considerable exactness. There is, for instance, the Paccari-tampu myth. It is told by Garcilasso de la Vega, Cieza de Leon, Betanzos, Balboa, Morua, Montesinos, Salcamayhua and Sarmiento, all agreeing sufficiently closely to prove that precisely the same tradition had been handed down, with the same details, to their various informants. Similarly the details of the Chanca war and other principal events were preserved.

'The Amautas composed both tragedies and comedies, which were represented before the Inca and his court on solemn occasions. The subject matter of the tragedy related to military deeds and the victories of former times; while the arguments of the comedies were on agricultural and familiar household subjects. They understood the composition of long and short verses, with the right number of syllables in each. They did not use rhymes in the verses.'

Atahualpa was still in the litter when the first gun went off.

The sound struck the square of Cajamarca and came back from the low adobe walls. Pigeons lifted from the roofs. Men in the crowd flinched, though many had never heard a cannon before; the bearers of the litter bent under it, and the gold ornaments hanging from its frame rang against one another. Atahualpa turned his head toward the noise. He was seated beneath a canopy of feathers, his hair held by the royal llautu, with a red fringe falling across his forehead. Around him stood nobles in fine cloth, attendants carrying vessels, musicians, and soldiers who had come into the city without their weapons because the strangers had asked to meet their lord in peace.

It was the afternoon of 16 November 1532. Francisco Pizarro had placed his men in the buildings around the plaza and hidden the horses behind the walls. Hernando Pizarro and Hernando de Soto waited with cavalry in the side streets. Pedro de Candia had the guns. Friar Vicente de Valverde came out to meet the Inca, carrying a breviary and a cross.

Atahualpa watched him approach.

Valverde spoke through the interpreter, Felipillo, telling the Inca that he must accept the Christian faith and the authority of the king of Spain. The friar offered him the book. Atahualpa took it, turned it in his hands, and held it to his ear. It made no sound. He opened it, looked at the marks on the pages, and dropped it onto the ground.

Valverde went back toward Pizarro, calling that the Inca had thrown down the word of God. The order passed quickly among the Spaniards. The horsemen tightened their reins. Match cords glowed beside the guns. From the roofs and doorways, men who had hidden there began to step into the open.

Atahualpa had come to Cajamarca after defeating his brother Huáscar in the war for the throne. His army lay outside the city, spread through the valley and along the roads from the north. He had reason to believe that the bearded foreigners were few. They had entered the country asking questions, accepting gifts, and sending messages of friendship. The Inca had seen their horses, but he had not yet seen what men mounted on them could do in a confined square.

The cannon fired.

Smoke rolled low across the plaza. Horses burst from the passages, their iron shoes striking sparks from the stones. The soldiers surrounding Atahualpa tried to lift the litter higher, but the crowd pressed inward and the bearers stumbled. Spaniards cut at them with swords. Some reached for the cords and poles; others fell beneath the litter, trampled by their own people. The nobles called out that the Inca must not touch the ground.

Pizarro rode toward him on foot. One of the Spaniards fired a harquebus over the heads of the crowd. The noise broke the formation entirely. Men ran for the walls, for the entrances, for the open country beyond the city. Those nearest the litter pushed against one another so fiercely that the wall at one side of the plaza gave way. Bodies spilled through the breach.

Atahualpa remained seated while the bearers changed beneath him. One Spaniard reached up with his sword. Pizarro caught the blade with his hand and took the cut across his arm. Then the litter tipped. Pizarro and several soldiers seized the Inca together, dragging him down before he could be crushed beneath it.

By his own account, Cieza de León wrote that he endured the country and its dangers while following his captain, saying that “Neither fatigue nor the ruggedness of the country, nor the mountains and rivers, nor intolerable hunger and suffering, have ever been sufficient to obstruct my two duties, namely, writing and following my flag and my captain without fault.” He was not at Cajamarca that day; he learned the event from men who had been there and from the accounts that followed the army south. Garcilaso, writing later from Spain, preserved another memory of the seizure: Atahualpa asking why the strangers had attacked him after he had entered the city without weapons.

The fighting did not stop when the Inca was taken. Men still fled across the square. Spaniards pursued them among the dead and seized ornaments from the fallen. The royal litter lay broken on the stones, its cloth torn, its golden fittings scattered beneath the feet of the horses.

Atahualpa was carried into a room in the house where Pizarro had established himself. His wrists were bound. Outside, the plaza filled with abandoned sandals, snapped poles, blood, and feathers. The gates were closed against the army waiting beyond Cajamarca.

Peter Hagendorf was in the street before the Neustadt gate when the first houses caught fire.

It was 20 May 1631, the tenth by the old calendar, and the morning had begun with smoke along the eastern wall. The imperial troops had entered Magdeburg after the breach was opened, Pappenheim’s men pressing through with their pikes levelled and their matchcords glowing at the ends. Hagendorf carried his musket under one arm and a short sword at his hip. He had slept badly in a ditch outside the city and had eaten a crust of bread softened in beer. Now the street was full of people running westward, some barefoot, some carrying bundles, some carrying nothing.

A woman came out of a doorway with a child against her breast. Behind her a man dragged a chest by its iron handles. The chest struck the paving stones at each step. A soldier seized the man by the collar and kicked him away from it. The lid sprang open. Linen spilled into the street, followed by a brass candlestick and three silver spoons.

“Leave it,” Hagendorf said.

The soldier did not look at him. He thrust the spoons into his coat.

At the corner of the street stood a wagon loaded with barrels. One barrel had split, and beer ran between the stones, black in the soot. Two soldiers knelt beside it, drinking from their helmets. Beyond them the houses burned with a dry, cracking sound. The upper floors leaned over the street, their beams already bright beneath the plaster. A man in a black coat came out of the smoke with blood on his cheek and a large key ring in his hand. He stopped when he saw the soldiers.

Hagendorf would have remembered the ring because it was so large: iron keys, brass keys, a little wooden tag tied to one of them. The man held it out as though it might still purchase his life.

“Take me to the commander,” he said.

The nearest soldier struck him with the butt of his musket. The man fell beside the wagon. His keys scattered. One rolled under Hagendorf’s boot.

He picked it up and put it in his pocket.

Near the cathedral, the crowd thickened. Magdeburg’s citizens had gathered there because the stone walls seemed safer than the timber houses, and because the pastors had told them that the churches would be spared. Smoke had settled beneath the vaults. Horses screamed outside. Somewhere beyond the cloister a bell rang three times, stopped, then began again.

A councillor named Otto von Guericke moved through the press with his hands raised, trying to keep people from crushing one another at the door. His face was grey with ash. He had lost his hat and wore only one shoe. Behind him came a maid carrying a small child wrapped in a tablecloth.

Hagendorf saw a woman kneeling before an altar, her mouth moving without sound. A soldier pulled the silver ornaments from the altar cloth. Another fired into the air to clear a path. The report struck the stone and came back in a hard redoubled crack. Pigeons burst from the roof beams. People screamed and fell against one another.

By noon the smoke hid the sun. The city gates were shut, then opened, then shut again as men drove cattle through them. The streets ran with water from overturned tubs and with blood from the slaughterhouse. Hagendorf found his company near the market, where a wagon of powder had been unloaded beneath the arcade. Its barrels were marked with the imperial eagle. A corporal ordered them carried to the river, but no one obeyed; there were too many houses burning and too many rooms left to search.

On a step outside a merchant’s house, Hagendorf found a folded paper blackened at one edge. The ink was still legible. It contained verses by Friedrich von Logau, the Silesian who wrote under the name Salomon von Golaw, lines copied in a neat clerk’s hand about the world turned upside down by war. Hagendorf could not read all of it. He held the page close to the light, sounded out the name, and tucked it inside his coat beside the iron key.

Then a boy ran from the house shouting that the powder had caught.

The blast lifted the arcade roof. Stones and burning wood came down into the market. Men dropped their muskets and covered their heads. A horse broke its tether and plunged through the smoke. Hagendorf fell against the fountain, the paper still pressed beneath his coat, while the barrels burned and the market disappeared in fire.

The cotton plants came out of the ground at Nandete on 20 July 1905.

Men worked along the rows with hoes and short-handled digging sticks, loosening the red soil around the stems before pulling. The plants had been ordered into the fields by the German district office, and each household was expected to tend them as well as its own food. The cotton was thin after the rains failed. Its leaves were dusted brown, and the bolls had opened unevenly, some no larger than a child’s fist. A headman stood beside the field with a list of names. He had a German demand behind him and the village behind him, and kept looking from one to the other.

At Ngarambe, several miles away, Kinjikitile Ngwale had been telling people that the water of the spirits would turn German bullets into water. He had received the message, as he said, from Hongo, the snake-spirit who lived in the river. The liquid was kept in a gourd and carried from settlement to settlement. Kinjikitile dipped his fingers into it and touched the forehead or chest of each person who came before him. The word for water was repeated until it became the name of the rising: maji.

“Maji,” the people said.

They came carrying calabashes, spears, bows, and bottles stoppered with grass. Some had walked from the Matumbi hills through the night. Others had left fields where the cotton stood under orders from the German authorities. Kinjikitile wore the long white cloth of a ritual specialist. By his own account, he had been instructed to unite the peoples who had been divided by chiefs, languages, and the boundaries of German administration. On that day he held the gourd above the crowd and told them that the medicine would protect them.

The promise was exact. Bullets would become water.

A few days later, the first attacks began against the cotton stations and the men who guarded them. In the coastal districts, African policemen carried the news along the roads faster than the district officers could send reports. Cotton was burned. Government stores were broken open. Some headmen joined the rebellion; others hid their tax registers or fled toward the mission stations. A German official at Kilwa wrote of villages emptied at the approach of armed men. Another report counted the dead in the language of administration: Europeans, askari, porters, rebels.

The German response moved from the coast inland.

At Mahenge, Lieutenant Gustav von Hassel had fewer than two hundred men at first, including African soldiers of the Schutztruppe and their porters. The town stood on a rise above the surrounding country, with the boma, storehouses, and mission buildings gathered inside a rough defensive line. Beyond it were fields, palms, and the paths by which the rebels came. In October, the force attacking Mahenge grew to several thousand. They advanced in dense formations, carrying spears and shields, with drums sounding behind them. Their leaders had distributed the medicine. They had been told that the rifles would fail.

On the morning of 30 October 1905, the grass beyond the town was wet with the last night’s rain. German sentries saw movement on the slopes and fired. The first volleys tore gaps in the advancing lines. Men fell, and the others closed over them. They came on shouting “Maji! Maji!” and striking their shields with their spear shafts.

Hassel ordered the machine gun to the front.

The weapon was a Maxim, mounted where its crew could sweep the open ground below the rise. Its belt fed steadily while the riflemen fired over one another’s shoulders. The attack reached the outer ditch. Men climbed the earthwork and were shot down at the crest. Others threw themselves flat among the grass, then rose again when the firing slackened. The water medicine was still on their bodies, in gourds tied at the waist and in marks painted across the chest.

By afternoon the slope was covered with bodies.

The German report recorded that the attack had been repulsed and that the enemy had suffered heavy losses. The surviving fighters withdrew toward the villages and forest tracks. After them came the patrols. Crops were cut down, granaries burned, and settlements that could not provide food or taxes were cleared. Women, children, and old men moved into the bush with what they could carry. The rains came, and there was less to eat.

At Ngarambe, Kinjikitile’s gourd was taken from him when the Germans arrested him. The rope was prepared, and he was hanged.
